title: Expressions Deep Dive: Lists, Tuples & Nested Expressions
subtitle: Lists and tuples are Python's two main sequence types. The 2024/2025 exam directly asked students to compare them (Q1a). The nested expression in Q1d (the grading formula) is also this week's territory.
learningOutcome: Lists and tuples are Python's two main sequence types. The 2024/2025 exam directly asked students to compare them (Q1a). The nested expression in Q1d (the grading formula) is also this week's territory.

content.text: A list is a mutable, ordered collection. Created with square brackets []. You can change, add, or remove elements.
my_list = [7, 8, 10] my_list[0] = 99 # Change first element print(my_list) # [99, 8, 10] my_list.append(5) # Add to end print(my_list) # [99, 8, 10, 5]

content.text: A tuple is an immutable, ordered collection. Created with parentheses (). Once created, cannot be changed.
my_tuple = (7, 8, 10) print(my_tuple[0]) # 7 (indexing works) my_tuple[0] = 99 # TypeError! Cannot modify tuple
A list is like a shopping cart (you can add/remove items). A tuple is like a printed receipt (fixed forever after printing).

content.text: Similarities: Both store multiple items. Both support indexing. Both can hold mixed data types. Both support for loops.

Syntax: Lists use [] · Tuples use () Mutability: Lists are mutable (elements can change) · Tuples are immutable (cannot change after creation) Performance: Tuples are slightly faster (less overhead) Use case: Lists for data that changes · Tuples for fixed data (coordinates, RGB values)
my_list = [7, 8, 10] my_list[0] = 99 # Works! Now [99, 8, 10] my_tuple = (7, 8, 10) my_tuple[0] = 99 # TypeError! Cannot modify

content.text: A nested expression is an expression inside another expression. Python evaluates the innermost part first.

test_score = float(input("Test score (max 55): ")) assignment_score = float(input("Assignment (max 10): ")) attendance = float(input("Attendance %: ")) final_score = (test_score + (2 * assignment_score)) / 3 + (5 if attendance >= 90 else 0) print("Final Score:", final_score) # Example: test=45, assignment=8, attendance=92 # (45 + 16) / 3 + 5 = 61/3 + 5 = 20.33 + 5 = 25.33
Common mistake — Confusing [] (list) with () (tuple). Also: the conditional expression (ternary) — write value_if_true if condition else value_if_false , not the other way round.
